title: tcpdump
description: The classic command-line packet capture and filtering tool built on libpcap, using Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax. Simpler and more universally available than tshark for quick captures and scripting.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
Current stable is **tcpdump 4.99.6** (Dec 2025), paired with **libpcap 1.10.x**; a 5.0 release has been in progress but not yet shipped as of late 2026.

## 1. Install

```bash
sudo pacman -S tcpdump
```

## 2. Run without full root, via capabilities

```bash
sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin=eip $(command -v tcpdump)
```

After this, your normal user can capture without `sudo` (though writing to some system paths may still need it). Verify with `getcap $(command -v tcpdump)`.

## 3. First capture

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i wlan0 -c 10
```

Prints one line per packet with source/destination and a protocol summary. See [BPF Filters](/tcpdump/bpf-filters/) for narrowing this down.
Getting Started.BPF Filters:
tcpdump filters use Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax — the same language tshark's `-f` capture filter accepts, and worth learning once since it transfers directly.

## Primitives

| Primitive | Example |
| --- | --- |
| `host` | `host 10.0.0.5` |
| `net` | `net 10.0.0.0/24` |
| `port` | `port 443` |
| `portrange` | `portrange 8000-8010` |
| `src` / `dst` | `src host 10.0.0.5` |
| `tcp` / `udp` / `icmp` | `tcp and port 22` |

## Combining with logic

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp and (port 80 or port 443) and not src host 10.0.0.1'
```

`and`, `or`, `not` (or `&&`, `||`, `!`) compose primitives; quote the whole expression so the shell doesn't interpret the parentheses.

## Byte-offset matching

```bash
sudo tcpdump 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'
```

Matches only TCP SYN packets — raw byte-offset filters let you match arbitrary flag bits when there's no named primitive for it.
Getting Started.Reading And Writing Captures:
## Write to a file

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap 'port 443'
```

`-w` writes raw packets (not human-readable text) — this is the format tshark and Wireshark both read natively.

## Read back later

```bash
tcpdump -r capture.pcap -n
```

`-n` disables DNS/hostname resolution, which both speeds up reading and avoids the noise of resolver lookups changing output between runs.

## Verbosity levels

| Flag | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| (none) | One-line summary |
| `-v` | + TTL, ID, total length, checksum |
| `-vv` | + more protocol-specific detail |
| `-vvv` | + full detail (e.g. complete NFS packet contents) |
| `-x` | Hex dump of packet (excluding link-level header) |
| `-X` | Hex + ASCII dump |
| `-A` | Print packet payload as ASCII only |

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A 'tcp port 80'
```

Good for a quick eyeball of unencrypted HTTP traffic without a full protocol dissector.

Guides.Rotating Captures:
For always-on captures on a storage-constrained box, tcpdump has its own rotation flags — no external `logrotate` needed.

## Time-based rotation

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w '/var/log/pcap/cap-%Y%m%d-%H%M%S.pcap' \
  -G 3600 -W 24
```

`-G 3600` starts a new file every hour; `-W 24` keeps at most 24 files (one day), deleting the oldest as new ones are created. The `%Y%m%d-%H%M%S` in `-w` is a strftime pattern, substituted per file.

## Size-based rotation

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /var/log/pcap/cap.pcap -C 100 -W 10
```

`-C 100` rotates every 100 MB instead of by time; combine `-C` with `-G` to rotate on whichever limit hits first.

*Part of the [BPF Filters](/tcpdump/bpf-filters/) page.* Quick script to watch outbound DNS queries only.

Source: `example/watch_dns.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

IFACE="${1:-eth0}"

sudo tcpdump -i "$IFACE" -n -l 'udp port 53' \
  | grep --line-buffered 'A?'
```

Run it:

```bash
chmod +x example/watch_dns.sh
./example/watch_dns.sh wlan0
```

CLI Reference.tcpdump:
## Synopsis

```
tcpdump [options] [expression]
```

## Common options

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-D` | List available capture interfaces |
| `-i <iface>` | Interface to capture on; `any` for all |
| `-w <file>` | Write raw packets to a file |
| `-r <file>` | Read packets from a file |
| `-n` / `-nn` | Disable name / name+port resolution |
| `-c <n>` | Stop after `n` packets |
| `-G <sec>` | Rotate `-w` output file every `sec` seconds |
| `-C <MB>` | Rotate `-w` output file every `MB` megabytes |
| `-W <n>` | Keep at most `n` rotated files |
| `-s <bytes>` | Snapshot length (bytes captured per packet); `0` = full |
| `-v`, `-vv`, `-vvv` | Increasing verbosity |
| `-x` / `-X` | Hex / hex+ASCII payload dump |
| `-A` | ASCII payload dump |
| `-e` | Print link-level (Ethernet) header |
| `-l` | Line-buffer stdout (for piping to `grep`, `tee`, etc.) |

Full manual: `man tcpdump`; filter syntax details: `man pcap-filter`.

Project.FAQ:
### `tcpdump: <iface>: You don't have permission to capture on that device`

Either run with `sudo`, or set capabilities once as shown in [Getting Started](/tcpdump/getting-started/) so your normal user can capture directly.

### Captured packets are truncated

The default snapshot length historically truncated packets to 262144 bytes in modern tcpdump (older defaults were 68 or 96 bytes and *did* commonly truncate). If you still see truncation, pass `-s 0` explicitly to capture full packets regardless of size.

### tshark reads my `.pcap` fine but some other tool rejects it

By default tcpdump writes the older `pcap` format, not `pcapng`. If a downstream tool expects pcapng specifically, convert with `editcap in.pcap out.pcapng` (from the `wireshark-cli`/`tshark` package).
